content: 1. Manzano-Robleda et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2015 to evaluate the efficacy of boceprevir and telaprevir in treating chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection caused by genotype 1. Their findings were published in Annals of Hepatology. 2. Ambrosino et al. explored the association between viral hepatitis and the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies through a systematic review and meta-analysis, with their results appearing in Digestive and Liver Disease in 2015. 3. Khodabandehloo and Roshani performed a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2014 to determine the prevalence of HCV genotypes among Iranian patients, as published in Hepatitis Monthly. 4. In 2013, Khodabandehloo, Roshani, and Sayehmiri analyzed the prevalence and trends of HCV infection among blood donors in Iran through a systematic review and meta-analysis, with their findings published in the Journal of Research in Medical Sciences. 5. Khuroo et al. assessed the diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care tests for HCV infection in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PloS One in 2015. 6. Shivkumar et al. evaluated the accuracy of rapid and point-of-care screening tests for HCV through a systematic review and meta-analysis, with their findings published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2012. 7. Whiting et al. introduced the QUADAS-2 tool in 2011, a revised instrument for assessing the quality of diagnostic accuracy studies, as detailed in Annals of Internal Medicine. 8. Bossuyt et al. elaborated on the STARD statement, which provides guidelines for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies, in a publication in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2003. 9. Al-Tahish et al. evaluated the effectiveness of three types of rapid tests for detecting HCV antibodies among blood donors in Alexandria, Egypt, with their findings published in Journal of Virological Methods in 2013. 10. Bonacini et al. investigated the impact of coexisting HIV-1 infection on the diagnosis and evaluation of HCV in a study published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2001. 11. Buti et al. developed a rapid method for detecting anti-HCV antibodies in patients with chronic hepatitis C, as reported in Revista Española de Enfermedades Digestivas in 2000. 12. Caudai et al. examined the correlation between antibody testing and RT-PCR results in HCV infection, particularly focusing on HCV-RNA detection in PBMCs of plasma viremia-negative, HCV-seropositive individuals, as published in Infection in 1998. 13. Cha et al. evaluated the performance of the OraQuick HCV rapid antibody test, with their findings published in Annals of Laboratory Medicine in 2013. 14. Croom et al. adapted a commercial enzyme immunoassay for detecting HCV antibodies in dried blood spots, as detailed in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2006. 15. Da Rosa et al. assessed the diagnostic performance of two point-of-care tests for anti-HCV detection, with their findings published in Hepatitis Monthly in 2013. 16. Daniel et al. evaluated a rapid assay as an alternative to conventional enzyme immunoassays for detecting HCV-specific antibodies, as reported in Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2005. 17. Denoyel et al. assessed the performance of a new HCV assay on the Bayer ADVIA Centaur Immunoassay System, as published in Clinical Laboratory in 2004. 18. Dokubo et al. compared HCV RNA and antibody detection in dried blood spots and plasma specimens, with their findings published in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2014. 19. Drobnik et al. highlighted the public health implications of rapid HCV screening using oral swabs in community-based organizations serving high-risk populations, as detailed in American Journal of Public Health in 2011. 20. Eroglu et al. developed a highly sensitive and specific enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detecting HCV antibodies, as published in Acta Virologica in 2000. 21. Feucht et al. conducted a study on the reliability of commercially available HCV antibody tests, with their findings published in Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 1995. 22. Hess et al. evaluated the sensitivity and specificity of point-of-care rapid combination tests for syphilis, HIV, and HCV, as reported in PloS One in 2014. 23. Hui et al. assessed a new rapid whole-blood serological test for HCV, with their findings published in Acta Virologica in 2002. 24. Ibrahim et al. evaluated the accuracy of a rapid oral HCV diagnostic test among a Saudi sample, as detailed in Clinical Oral Investigations in 2015. 25. Ivantes et al. reported a high prevalence of HCV associated with familial history in a small town in southern Brazil and evaluated the efficiency of a rapid test for epidemiological surveys, as published in Brazilian Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2010. 26. Jewett et al. assessed the field-based performance of three pre-market rapid HCV antibody assays among young adults who inject drugs in San Diego, CA, as reported in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2012. 27. Kant et al. evaluated a rapid on-site anti-HCV test as a screening tool for HCV infection, with their findings published in European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2013. 28. Kaur et al. evaluated rapid kits for detecting HIV, HBsAg, and HCV infections, as reported in Indian Journal of Medical Sciences in 2000. 29. Kim et al. assessed a new rapid test kit for detecting HCV infection, with their findings published in Journal of Virological Methods in 2013. 30. Kosack et al. evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of the ImmunoFlow HCV rapid immunochromatographic test for detecting HCV antibodies, as detailed in Journal of Virological Methods in 2014. 31. Lakshmi et al. evaluated a third-generation anti-HCV enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay in patients undergoing hemodialysis, as published in Indian Journal of Medical Microbiology in 2007. 32. Larrat et al. assessed the performance of an antigen-antibody combined assay for HCV testing without venipuncture, as reported in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2012. 33. Lee et al. conducted a multi-center evaluation of a new rapid test for detecting HCV infection using whole blood, serum, plasma, and oral fluid, as published in Journal of Hepatology in 2010. 34. Lee et al. evaluated a new rapid test for detecting HCV infection suitable for use with blood or oral fluid, as detailed in Journal of Virological Methods in 2011. 35. Lee et al. assessed a rapid, point-of-care test device for diagnosing HCV infection, with their findings published in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2010. 36. Maity et al. evaluated the performance and diagnostic usefulness of commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays and rapid kits for detecting HIV, HBV, and HCV in India, as reported in Virology Journal in 2012. 37. Montebugnoli et al. developed a rapid test for visually detecting anti-HCV antibodies in whole blood, as published in Clinica Chimica Acta in 1999. 38. Mvere et al. reported encouraging results from rapid and simple hepatitis assays in a blood donor population in Zimbabwe, as detailed in Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 1996. 39. Nalpas et al. investigated HCV viremia and anti-HCV antibodies in alcoholics, with their findings published in Journal of Hepatology in 1992. 40. Njouom et al. proposed a cost-effective algorithm for diagnosing HCV infection and predicting HCV viremia in Cameroon, as reported in Journal of Virological Methods in 2006. 41. Nyirenda et al. studied the prevalence of HBV and HCV infections and their coinfection with HIV among medical inpatients in Malawi, as published in Journal of Infection in 2008. 42. O'Connell et al. evaluated rapid test kits for detecting HCV antibodies for use in pre-donation screening in emergency settings, as detailed in Transfusion in 2013. 43. O'Flynn et al. assessed a new HCV assay on the Abbott AxSYM random access analyzer, as published in Clinical Laboratory in 1997. 44. Park et al. evaluated the performance of the Vitros anti-HCV antibody assay for use in clinical laboratories, as reported in Clinical Biochemistry in 2012. 45. Poovorawan et al. compared the detection of HCV antibodies using a rapid HCV test, ELISA, and immunoblot, as published in Southeast Asian Journal of Tropical Medicine and Public Health in 1994. 46. Prayson et al. applied a second-generation recombinant immunoblot assay to assess HCV infection, as detailed in Laboratory Medicine in 1993. 47. Rihn et al. evaluated a supplemental assay for diagnosing HCV infections, as published in International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2000. 48. Scalioni et al. assessed the performance of rapid HCV antibody assays among highand low-risk populations, as reported in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2014. 49. Smith et al. evaluated three rapid screening assays for detecting HCV antibodies, as published in Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2011. 50. Smith et al. assessed the performance of premarket rapid HCV antibody assays in four national HIV behavioral surveillance system sites, as detailed in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2011. 51. Sommese et al. compared screening and confirmatory serological assays in blood donors in southern Italy, as published in Journal of Clinical Laboratory Analysis in 2014. 52. Tagny et al. compared an antigen/antibody combination assay with a rapid test for screening HCV infection in a high-prevalence country, as reported in Journal of Virological Methods in 2014. 53. Vrielink et al. evaluated the performance of a new third-generation anti-HCV ELISA (Monolisa anti-HCV new antigens) in various serum panels, as published in Vox Sanguinis in 1995. 54. Vrielink et al. assessed the sensitivity and specificity of three third-generation anti-HCV ELISAs, as detailed in Vox Sanguinis in 1995. 55. Yaari et al. developed a simple and rapid test for detecting HCV salivary antibodies, as published in Journal of Virological Methods in 2006. 56. Yang et al. evaluated the performance characteristics of a combined HCV core antigen and anti-HCV antibody test in different patient groups, as reported in Kaohsiung Journal of Medical Sciences in 2011. 57. Yang et al. compared the performance of the newly developed Elecsys anti-HCV II assay with other widely used assays, as published in Clinica Chimica Acta in 2013. 58. Yoo et al. evaluated the Elecsys Anti-HCV II assay for routine HCV screening in different Asian Pacific populations and for detecting early infection, as reported in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2015. 59. Yuen et al. assessed the accuracy of the SM-HCV rapid test for detecting HCV antibodies, as published in American Journal of Gastroenterology in 2001. 60. Alter et al. provided guidelines for laboratory testing and result reporting of HCV antibodies, as detailed in MMWR Recommendations and Reports in 2003. 61. The World Health Organization published guidelines for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with HCV infection, accessible as of June 6, 2016. 62. St. John and Price reviewed the economic evidence and implications of point-of-care testing, as published in Clinical Biochemistry Reviews in 2013. 63. Parisi et al. discussed recent advances in point-of-care testing for HCV infection and its implications for alternative screening strategies, as reported in New Microbiologica in 2014. 64. Schünemann et al. outlined methods for grading the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations for diagnostic tests and strategies, as published in BMJ in 2008. 65. Shepard et al. reviewed the global epidemiology of HCV infection, as detailed in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2005. 66. Leeflang et al. examined bias in sensitivity and specificity caused by data-driven selection of optimal cutoff values, as published in Clinical Chemistry in 2008. 67. Irwig et al. discussed meta-analytic methods for diagnostic test accuracy, as reported in Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 1995. 68. Rothstein et al. edited a book on publication bias in meta-analysis, focusing on prevention, assessment, and adjustments, published by John Wiley & Sons in 2005.
